doc.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in northern England
title: Local reaction to jazz and British bands of the 1930s
summary: A girl's father stares as Pug sings along to a record; she notes England had good bands in the 1930s and visiting Americans.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I think it’s so great that Bessie Smith lands in the north of England and falls on someone’s ears like that. I just love that story.

Well I think it’s unusual. I mean my father said, “She’s jazz crazy you know.” And I can remember going to someone’s home and she’d bought some records, she had a brother in the RAF or something like that, and invited me to go around, and I sort of, I remember going into the house, and the girl’s father was sitting there having his tea, which is like dinner for us, for the working man. And he was sitting there sort of digging into his tea and this girl put on the record, the phonograph you know, wound it up. And I started

doing this kind of thing. I mean and this man’s looking at me like I had descended from another planet. I mean again, they didn’t understand. Because jazz music was really a very esoteric type of sound. We’ve had good bands incidentally in England. I mean don’t forget that Coleman Hawkins and the Ramblers, the Dutch Ramblers and stuff, the big bands of the ‘30s, Henry Hall, Ambrose Roy Fox, Jack Hilton and so on, had some very good bands, and they had good support from the American musicians that chose to come over there. You know, Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter.
